frameworks.name: Three Strategic Buckets
frameworks.definition: Every business allocates resources into three categories: acquiring more customers, increasing customer lifetime value, and decreasing operational risk.

claims.text: Business growth is determined by three independent levers: customer acquisition volume, lifetime gross profit per customer, and risk mitigation. Optimizing any one lever independently grows the business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The allocation rule across the three buckets follows a 70-20-10 distribution: 70% to customer acquisition and value-per-customer improvements, 20% toward future-proofing, and 10% to new capability building.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: When shifting resources to develop new channels or capabilities (e.g., expanding from YouTube to emerging platforms), do not reassign the top performers from the existing core business. Reallocating core talent to new initiatives sacrifices current performance without guaranteeing success in the new domain.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: expanding to new channels or platforms
claims.mechanism: Core performers lack the capability-building mindset required for unproven initiatives; reallocating them creates opportunity cost in the proven business before new performance scales.
bounded_by: Does not apply when new capability is directly adjacent to core competency
Does not apply when core business is declining

claims.text: A founder's primary competitive advantage as CEO is decision-making authority: the ability to allocate resources, say yes immediately without committee approval, and override process to prioritize urgent strategic needs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founder can write checks and make unilateral calls; team members must navigate committee approval, process, and consensus, resulting in slower execution.
bounded_by: Does not apply when founder has ceded decision authority to board or investors
Advantage diminishes as organization grows and CEO must delegate approval authority

claims.text: Strategy is a synonym for prioritization: choosing which unlimited opportunities to fund given limited resources.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Businesses mature through predictable revenue-stage transitions: each stage ($0-$1M, $1M-$10M, $10M+) presents distinct constraint types and requires different operational solutions. This 10-stage roadmap applies across software, physical products, service businesses, and brick-and-mortar.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each revenue stage introduces new constraints (hiring, systems, capital) that previous stages did not require; solutions learned at one stage must be modified for the next.

claims.text: The primary unfairness in founder advantage is not knowledge or effort—it is asymmetric decision authority and immediate resource allocation compared to professional managers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: team operates under process approval requirements

practices.text: When allocating resources to future capabilities or platform shifts, explicitly staff with new hires who have capability-building orientation rather than core-business execution expertise.
Establish explicit resource allocation rules at the start of each planning period: define percentages for acquisition, value-per-customer, and risk initiatives before committing capital.
Use the 10-stage revenue roadmap to diagnose current constraint severity and identify the specific operational solution required at your current stage.
As a founder, leverage your decision-authority advantage by identifying bottleneck decisions (ones requiring immediate yes/no calls) and solving them before team consensus can form.
